units.title: 1. Brainstem Anatomy and Crossed Hemiplegia
units.guide:
The brainstem runs rostral (midbrain), central (pons) and caudal (medulla) between brain and spinal cord.
Its hallmark presentation is crossed hemiplegia: ipsilateral LMN cranial nerve palsy plus contralateral hemiplegia, because the corticospinal tract decussates while the cranial nerve nucleus is lesioned ipsilaterally.
The note contrasts hallmark presentations at other sites: cortical lesions give aphasia and internal capsule lesions give contralateral UMN 7th nerve palsy.

units.title: 2. Midline 4M and Lateral 4S
units.guide:
Brainstem structures divide by position: the midline 4M are the motor nuclei of CN 3, 4, 6 and 12, the medial longitudinal fasciculus (lesion → internuclear ophthalmoplegia), the medial lemniscus (posterior column fibres after decussation at the medulla) and the motor tract (corticospinal).
The lateral 4S are the spinothalamic tract, spinocerebellar fibres, sympathetic fibres (lesion → Horner's syndrome) and the spinal nucleus of the trigeminal nerve carrying sensory fibres.
This medial-lateral map predicts which tracts each brainstem syndrome spares or involves.

units.title: 3. Midbrain Anatomy
units.guide:
The anterior view shows the crus cerebri of the midbrain bounded by the interpeduncular fossa with the oculomotor nerve exiting between the crura, above the pons; posteriorly the tectum carries the superior and inferior colliculi.
At the level of the superior colliculus the cross-section shows the cerebral aqueduct, oculomotor nucleus, MLF, red nucleus, substantia nigra, decussation of the rubrospinal tract and lemnisci, with the crus cerebri's middle 3/5th carrying corticospinal and corticonuclear fibres flanked by frontopontine fibres.
At the level of the inferior colliculus the trochlear nerve exits — the only cranial nerve to leave the brainstem posteriorly — with the mesencephalic nucleus of V, the decussation of the superior cerebellar peduncles and the temporoparietopontine fibre groups labelled.

units.title: 4. Ventral Midbrain Syndromes
units.guide:
Ventral midbrain syndromes share a vascular origin from the P1 segment of the posterior cerebral artery.
Weber's syndrome lesions the base of the midbrain (cerebral peduncle): CN-3 fibres plus corticospinal tract, giving ipsilateral 3rd nerve palsy with contralateral hemiplegia.
Claude's syndrome lesions the tegmentum: CN-3 fibres plus the red nucleus/superior cerebellar peduncle (dentato-rubro-thalamic fibres), giving ipsilateral 3rd nerve palsy with contralateral ataxia and tremor; Benedikt's syndrome combines both — extensive tegmentum plus base — adding the substantia nigra (nigrostriatal pathway) for contralateral hemichorea and hemiathetosis, printed as Weber + Claude.

units.title: 5. Dorsal Midbrain Syndromes
units.guide:
Dorsal midbrain (Parinaud's) syndrome is most commonly caused by pinealomas, lesioning the dorsum of midbrain — pretectal nucleus, periaqueductal grey matter and CN-3 fibres.
Its features are vertical gaze palsy (upgaze), sunsetting sign (looking down), Argyll Robertson pupil (accommodation present, light reflex absent), Collier's sign (levator palpebrae superioris overshoot → lid retraction), pseudo abducent pupil (printed as such), convergence-retraction nystagmus (overactive convergence centre) and skew deviation.
Nothnagel's syndrome is the anterior version of Parinaud's (CN-3 fibres plus superior cerebellar peduncle close to the red nucleus), the cerebellar peduncles connect superior→midbrain, middle→pons, inferior→medulla, and a note separates Parinaud's oculoglandular syndrome of tularemia (Francisella tularensis).

units.title: 6. Lateral Medullary (Wallenberg) Syndrome
units.guide:
Lateral medullary syndrome (Wallenberg's/PICA syndrome) arises from the V4 segment of the vertebral artery and PICA, usually by large vessel thrombosis or artery-to-artery infarction, with cardiac embolism printed as rare.
Higher mental functions and the motor system are normal; cranial nerves 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 12 are spared while the spinal nucleus of V gives hemifacial sensory loss, the vestibular nuclei give vertigo/ataxia/nystagmus, the NTS of VII impairs anterior 2/3rd taste, the nucleus ambiguus (IX, X) gives dysphagia with nasal regurgitation, the dorsal vagal nucleus gives autonomic symptoms and the cervical sympathetic chain gives ipsilateral Horner's.
Sensory findings are contralateral pain and temperature loss with posterior column sparing, and spinocerebellar fibres give ipsilateral cerebellar ataxia.

units.title: 7. Horner Syndrome Localisation
units.guide:
The Horner's diagram on this page localises the lesion along the three-neuron ophthalmosympathetic pathway.
A central (first-order) lesion gives central Horner syndrome, the printed example being Wallenberg syndrome; a preganglionic (second-order, C8-T1 to superior cervical ganglion) lesion's example is a Pancoast tumour; a postganglionic lesion travelling with the carotid artery gives carotid artery dissection, in which anhidrosis is absent because the sudomotor fibres leave with the external carotid.

units.title: 8. Medial Medullary Syndrome and Horizontal Gaze
units.sec: Medial Medullary Syndrome and Gaze Pathways
units.guide:
Medial medullary (Dejerine) syndrome involves the XII nerve nucleus (ipsilateral 12th palsy with paralysis and atrophy of one half of the tongue), the corticospinal tract (contralateral hemiplegia), the MLF (ipsilateral internuclear ophthalmoplegia) and the medial lemniscus (contralateral posterior column loss — touch and proprioception).
The horizontal gaze pathway runs from the frontal eye field to the contralateral PPRF and the VI nerve nucleus, whose internuclear fibres cross via the MLF to the opposite medial rectus subnucleus.
MLF lesion alone gives INO (ipsilateral adduction weakness with contralateral abduction nystagmus); MLF plus PPRF gives one-and-a-half syndrome; adding a VII palsy gives eight-and-a-half; bilateral VII palsy with one-and-a-half gives fifteen-and-a-half.

units.title: 9. Cruciate Paralysis and the Avellis-Jackson Table
units.guide:
Cruciate paralysis results from early decussation of upper limb fibres at the pyramidal decussation, presenting either as brachial diplegia (both arms weak with legs spared) or weakness of one arm and the opposite leg.
The note restates crossed hemiplegia as I/L LMN CN palsy plus C/L hemiplegia.
The Avellis versus Jackson table compares two medullary syndromes: both sit in the tegmentum of medulla; Avellis involves the X nerve and spinothalamic tract giving ipsilateral LMN X palsy with contralateral body pain-temperature loss and no weakness, while Jackson adds the hypoglossal nucleus for ipsilateral LMN XII palsy.

units.title: 10. Pontine Anatomy and Blood Supply
units.guide:
The dorsal pons cross-section labels 23 structures from the floor of the fourth ventricle down: cochlear and vestibular nuclei, abducens nucleus, nucleus prepositus hypoglossi and MLF on the median sulcus; raphe and pontine reticular formation in the tegmentum; spinal nucleus of V with its root, facial nucleus, lateral and superior olivary nuclei, lemnisci and central tegmental tract laterally; then the middle cerebellar peduncle, pontocerebellar fibres, corticospinal tract, pontine nuclei and basilar sulcus at the basis.
The printed note is that the pons has no tectum.
Blood supply is basilar artery for the majority, with lateral pons supplied by AICA plus basilar.

units.title: 11. Pontine Syndromes
units.guide:
The pontine syndrome table lists site, vascular origin and clinical features.
Millard-Gubler syndrome (ventral, basal pons, basilar artery) is ipsilateral LMN facial and sixth nerve palsies with contralateral hemiplegia — the FSH syndrome; Raymond syndrome is ipsilateral sixth nerve palsy with contralateral hemiplegia, printed as the SH syndrome.
Foville syndrome (dorsal tegmentum, basilar artery) adds ipsilateral conjugate gaze palsy (PPRF) to the Millard-Gubler picture — the FGH syndrome; Marie-Foix syndrome (lateral pons, AICA plus basilar) is ipsilateral ataxia (middle cerebellar peduncle), contralateral pain-temperature loss and contralateral hemiplegia — the ASH syndrome.
Locked-in syndrome follows bilateral extensive pontine infarction with an alert patient (reticular activating system normal), quadriplegia from corticospinal and corticobulbar lesions, and preserved vertical eye movements; top-of-basilar occlusion gives absent visual/oculomotor findings with bilateral medial temporal lobe features — behavioural change, fluctuating alertness, amnesia and visual hallucinations. Posterior stroke presents with the 5 D's: diplopia, dizziness, dystaxia, dysarthria and dysphagia.
